Every year Apple prepares a brand-new chip for its latest iPhone. However, the A20 Pro chip expected to power this autumn's iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Ultra sounds like it could be especially noteworthy. Here are two major upgrades generating significant buzz.

#1: A20 Pro will be the first iPhone chip built on a 2-nanometer process

Apple never fails to bring improvements with each new generation of chips. That much is beyond doubt. However, not every year brings upgrades of the same magnitude, and the anticipated A20 Pro chip is expected to stand out as a particularly impressive one.

The reason is that Apple will manufacture the A20 Pro using TSMC's latest 2-nanometer process.

Upgrading from the current 3-nanometer process to 2-nanometer means the A20 Pro can deliver greater performance while running more power-efficiently, with the chip size remaining roughly the same.

This kind of leap happens every time process technology takes a major step forward. That's precisely why Apple began laying the groundwork years ago, striving to secure priority access to TSMC's most cutting-edge fabrication processes in order to maintain its competitive edge in the chips used across the iPhone, iPad, Mac and other products.

We don't yet know which specific aspects of the A20 Pro Apple will focus on improving, but with the 2-nanometer process, this year's headroom for improvement will be greater than ever.

#2: Adopting Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module packaging for further performance gains

Beyond the advantages brought by the 2-nanometer process, the A20 Pro is also expected to gain another unique improvement through an innovative packaging technology known as Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM).

Here's a detailed explanation from my colleague Marcus:

According to reports, Apple is about to adopt WMCM packaging for the first time in an iPhone processor. WMCM allows different components, such as the SoC and DRAM, to be integrated directly at the wafer level before being cut into individual chips. The interconnect technology used eliminates the need for an interposer or substrate, bringing benefits in thermal management and signal integrity. In other words, Apple's next-generation chip won't just be smaller and more power-efficient thanks to the N2 process — it will also be physically closer to the device's memory, enabling better performance in workloads such as AI computation and high-end gaming, with power consumption also expected to drop further.

With WMCM on board, the A20 Pro is expected to perform particularly well on AI tasks. This comes as no surprise, given that iOS 27 itself is built around AI as its core focus.

What improvements are you most hoping to see on the iPhone 18 Pro? Let us know in the comments section.
